questionContent.content: A thin uniform square plate has mass $M$ and side $a$. Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane through one of its corners is:

explanation.content:
Centroidal MOI about the parallel axis, plus $M(\frac{\sqrt{2} a}{2})^2$ (parallel-axis theorem).

$I = \frac{2}{3}\,Ma^2$ (checked by direct integration).

A.why_students: Students start from the centroidal MOI about the wrong orientation (in-plane vs perpendicular to the plane).
A.why_wrong: For a lamina the in-plane and normal centroidal axes differ by the perpendicular-axis theorem; use the centroidal axis parallel to the asked axis.

B.why_students: Students quote the centroidal result and forget the axis is shifted.
B.why_wrong: The axis is at distance a/sqrt(2) from the centre: add M·(a/sqrt(2))².

C.why_students: Students take the full diameter/length (or the distance from the end) as the parallel-axis shift.
C.why_wrong: The shift in I = I_cm + Md² is the distance of the axis from the centre of mass.

D.why_wrong: The parallel-axis theorem adds Md² exactly once.

questionContent.content: A thin uniform circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has centre $O$. A circular hole of radius $R/3$ is cut from it, the centre $C$ of the hole being at distance $2R/3$ from $O$ (so the hole touches the rim). Here $M$ is the mass of the complete disc before the hole was cut. The moment of inertia of the remaining part about the diameter of the original disc that passes through $C$ is:

explanation.content:
Removed mass $m = M/9$ (area ratio). $I = I_{disc} - I_{hole}$, where $I_{hole}$ is the hole's centroidal MOI about the parallel axis plus $m\cdot$(distance of $C$ from the axis)$^2$.

$I = \frac{20}{81}\,MR^2$.

A.why_students: Students take the removed mass as M/3 (ratio of radii).
A.why_wrong: Mass of a uniform lamina scales with area: m = M/9.

C.why_students: Students subtract only m·OC² for the hole, treating it as a particle at C.
C.why_wrong: The removed disc has its own centroidal MOI that must also be subtracted.

D.why_students: Students add the MOI of the removed part instead of subtracting it.
D.why_wrong: The remaining body = full disc MINUS the removed disc.

questionContent.content: A thin uniform rod $OA$ has mass 3 kg and length 50 cm. A uniform solid sphere of mass 4 kg and radius 5 cm is rigidly attached at the end $A$ so that its centre lies on the line $OA$ produced, at a distance of 55 cm from $O$. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through $O$ perpendicular to the rod (and to the plane of rotation) is:

B.why_students: Students take the body's distance from O as the rod length L.
B.why_wrong: The body's centre is at L + r from O, not at the rod's end.

C.why_students: Students use ML²/12 for the rod even though the axis passes through its end.
C.why_wrong: About an end, a rod has I = ML²/3.

D.why_students: Students treat the attached body as a particle at its centre.
D.why_wrong: An extended body has its own centroidal MOI, added to m·d² by the parallel-axis theorem.

questionContent.content: Four particles, each of mass $m$, are placed at the vertices of a square $ABCD$ of side $a$ (held by a light rigid frame). The radius of gyration of the system about the line joining the mid-points of $AB$ and $CD$ is:

explanation.content: Perpendicular distances from the axis give $I = m\,(\frac{a}{2})^2 + m\,(\frac{a}{2})^2 + m\,(\frac{a}{2})^2 + m\,(\frac{a}{2})^2$. With $I = M_{total} k^2$: $k = \frac{1}{2}\,a$.

A.why_students: Students measure each particle's distance from a point on the axis instead of its perpendicular distance from the axis line.
A.why_wrong: Moment of inertia uses the perpendicular distance from the axis.

B.why_students: Students write k = I/M instead of k = √(I/M).
B.why_wrong: Radius of gyration is defined by I = M k², so k = √(I/M).

D.why_students: Students divide I by the mass of one particle instead of the total mass.
D.why_wrong: k² = I / (total mass of the system).

questionContent.content: A thin uniform circular ring of mass 1 kg and radius 15 cm is released from rest at the top of a rough inclined plane of inclination 30° and vertical height 2.5 m. It rolls down without slipping. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the speed (in m/s) of its centre when it reaches the bottom is ______.

explanation.content: $Mgh = \tfrac12 Mv^2(1 + I/MR^2)$ with $I/MR^2 = 1$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1+1)} = 5$ m/s.

questionContent.content: A thin uniform circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is placed on a rough inclined plane of inclination 30° and released. The minimum coefficient of static friction for which it rolls down without slipping is ($g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$):

explanation.content: $f = \dfrac{I/MR^2}{1 + I/MR^2}\,Mg\sin\theta$ and $f \le \mu Mg\cos\theta$ give $\mu_{min} = \dfrac{1}{1+1}\tan 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$.

A.why_students: Students take the normal reaction as Mg sinθ.
A.why_wrong: N = Mg cosθ on an incline.

C.why_students: Students use the no-sliding condition of a block, μ = tan θ.
C.why_wrong: A rolling body accelerates; friction only supplies the torque for α = a/R.

D.why_students: Students use the MOI of a different body.
D.why_wrong: Use this body's own I.

questionContent.content: A light string is wound round the rim of a pulley in the form of a thin ring (spokes of negligible mass) of mass 10 kg and radius 20 cm, free to rotate about a fixed horizontal frictionless axle through its centre. A block of mass 1 kg hangs from the free end of the string and the system is released from rest. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration of the block is:

explanation.content:
Block: $mg - T = ma$; pulley: $TR = I\alpha$ with $I = MR^2$; no slipping: $a = \alpha R$. Hence $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + I/R^2}$, $T = (I/R^2)a$, $\alpha = a/R$.

Answer: $0.9091\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

B.why_wrong: Torque arm and a = αR use the radius.

D.why_wrong: The block accelerates downward, so T < mg.

questionContent.content: A thin uniform rod of mass 2 kg and length 2.4 m is hinged at one end so that it can rotate freely in a vertical plane. It is held horizontal and released from rest. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the linear speed of its free end as it passes through the vertical position is:

explanation.content:
$I_O = \tfrac13 mL^2$. Energy: $\tfrac12 I_O\omega^2 = mg\tfrac L2 \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{3g/L}$; $v_{end} = \omega L$, $v_{cm} = \omega L/2$. At release $mg\tfrac L2 = I_O\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = \tfrac{3g}{2L}$.

Answer: $6 \sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

A.why_students: Students use ML²/12 although the rod turns about its end.
A.why_wrong: About an end, I = ML²/3.

B.why_students: Students take the fall of the centre of mass (and weight's arm) as the full length L.
B.why_wrong: The weight acts at the centre, L/2 from the hinge.

C.why_students: Students treat the rod as a particle at its free end.
C.why_wrong: Mass is spread along the rod: I = ML²/3 and the CM is at L/2.

questionContent.content: A uniform solid cylinder of mass 5 kg and radius 0.25 m is mounted on a fixed, frictionless horizontal axle through its centre (along its symmetry axis). explanation.content:
$I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$, $\tau = FR = I\alpha$, $\omega = \alpha t$, $W = \tfrac12 I\omega^2$, $P = \tau\omega$.
